messages.content: Write a three-paragraph encyclopedia-style overview of the history of postal systems.

Organised postal services are older than most people assume. Ancient Persia ran a relay network of mounted couriers along the Royal Road, where fresh horses waited at each station so that a message could cross the empire in about a week. The Roman cursus publicus later copied the idea, but it carried only official correspondence, and private letters travelled with merchants, soldiers or trusted friends. For centuries afterwards, ordinary people depended on such chance carriers, and a reply could take months.

The modern idea of a public post took shape in Europe between the fifteenth and eighteenth centuries. Families such as the Taxis built private networks that governments eventually took over, and a growing merchant class created steady demand for reliable delivery. Charges were usually paid by the recipient and depended on distance and on the number of sheets, which made letters expensive and encouraged people to write on both sides of the paper, in tiny handwriting.

Reform arrived in 1840 with the British penny post, in which the sender paid a flat fee, proved by an adhesive stamp. Volumes soared, other countries followed within a few years, and the Universal Postal Union later standardised international exchange. By the end of the nineteenth century, trains, steamships and sorting offices had turned the post into one of the first truly national networks.
